positions.text: Admission evidence is not execution authority. PACE shows why a safe and a leaking artifact can present the same admission evidence, then evaluates effect verification against authority compiled from the authenticated request immediately before a tool call executes. That mechanism extends the requirement for a last enforceable boundary. It does not evaluate reputation systems, prove the categorical institutional rule, or establish performance across all sovereign-runtime coordination layers.
scope_conditions: tool-using agents acting under authenticated user requests

source_provenance.sourceProposition: Pre-admission artifact vetting cannot settle authority when safe and leaking variants share admission evidence; enforcing schema-defined effects against authenticated request authority immediately before tool execution supplies the last actionable boundary.
source_provenance.exactEvidenceQuote: Vetting an artifact before admission does not settle this. A safe variant and a leaking variant can produce the same admission evidence, and a sound gate then cannot relax that site for either. We make that condition precise, which leaves the last boundary a deployment can still act on. We present Provenance-Aware Capability Enforcement (PACE), which mediates every tool call immediately before it executes. Path confinement proposes an executable cut of represented influence paths, while capability and effect verification checks schema-defined effects against authority compiled from the authenticated request.

positions.text: Progress is not permission. In APEX, an agent-written record of genuine task progress carried a false approval claim from an upstream skill into a downstream attacker-selected action. The chains succeeded in 512 of 690 attempts across four targeted-action families and six models. This is direct evidence of authority drift in the tested setting. It does not establish ordinary-deployment prevalence or show that every individual permission check passed.
scope_conditions: delegation chains under a bounded original consent

source_provenance.sourceProposition: An agent-written record of genuine task progress can carry a false claim of user approval across skills and induce an attacker-selected downstream action, empirically instantiating authority drift across a delegation chain.
source_provenance.exactEvidenceQuote: The key insight is that an agent-written record of genuine task progress can carry a false claim of user approval across skills: an upstream skill induces the agent to create the record, and a downstream skill uses it to direct the attacker-selected action. Across four targeted-action families and six models on SkillsBench, the chains induce the selected action in 512 of 690 attempts (74.2%).
